selection.method: highest remaining verified actor-primary profiles after Batch 30

profiles.name: Gloria Ann Simpson
profiles.excerpt: Gloria Ann Simpson was a radio and television actress whose surviving GRH work is strongest in NBC University Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Gloria Ann Simpson was born in Cleveland in 1900 and worked professionally in radio, television and film. Her screen credits place her in the same postwar West Coast acting community that supplied network radio with experienced supporting players.

Radio used Simpson most heavily in literary adaptation on NBC University Theater, with additional crime and suspense work on Rocky Fortune, Barrie Craig and The Whistler.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight NBC University Theater performances credited to Simpson, two Rocky Fortune appearances and additional broadcasts on Barrie Craig and The Whistler.

profiles.name: Harry Humphrey
profiles.excerpt: Harry Humphrey was a dependable Lux Radio Theatre stock actor whose supporting work helped populate major Hollywood adaptations.
profiles.bio_html:
Harry Humphrey is best documented through Lux Radio Theatre, where the weekly adaptation format depended on a regular supporting company around featured movie stars.

Surviving cast records show Humphrey handling small but necessary character roles, including judges and other authority figures, and also appearing on Dr. Christian. His work reflects the practical craft of radio stock acting rather than celebrity casting.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Humphrey and three Dr. Christian appearances.

profiles.name: Jack Kirkwood
profiles.excerpt: Jack Kirkwood carried vaudeville comedy into radio as both performer and host before moving into film and television.
profiles.bio_html:
Jack Kirkwood was born in Scotland in 1894 and built his early career in vaudeville before radio made him a familiar American comic personality.

Kirkwood hosted KFRC's Breakfast Club and later starred in The Jack Kirkwood Show, giving hosting a substantial place in his broadcasting career alongside acting and comedy. He later moved into film and television while continuing live performance.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine The Railroad Hour performances credited to Kirkwood, two Fibber McGee and Molly appearances and one CBS Radio Workshop broadcast.

profiles.name: Jerry Jarrett
profiles.excerpt: Jerry Jarrett was a recurring member of the wartime espionage repertory heard on Cloak and Dagger.
profiles.bio_html:
Jerry Jarrett is best documented in Golden Radio Hour through Cloak and Dagger, NBC's 1950 espionage anthology based on wartime intelligence operations.

The program shifted settings, identities and nationalities from week to week, demanding supporting actors who could establish characters quickly inside compact, documentary-influenced dramas. Jarrett's repeated casting places him firmly inside that repertory.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Cloak and Dagger performances credited to Jarrett, providing a concentrated record of his radio dramatic work.

profiles.name: John Ramsay Hill
profiles.excerpt: John Ramsay Hill brought a British voice and stage-trained character style to American literary radio and Hollywood comedy.
profiles.bio_html:
John Ramsay Hill worked in American radio as a British character actor during the postwar years. His surviving credits place him most often in formal literary adaptations and supporting roles that benefited from a cultivated English delivery.

He appeared repeatedly on NBC University Theater, with additional work on The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show and Escape. The contrast between those programs shows a performer able to move from prestige drama to comedy and suspense.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine NBC University Theater performances credited to Hill, two The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show appearances and one Escape broadcast.

profiles.name: Joseph Granby
profiles.excerpt: Joseph Granby carried a career from silent film and Broadway into radio and television, with a distinctive late-career voice role in It’s a Wonderful Life.
profiles.bio_html:
Joseph Granby was born in Boston in 1885 and began acting professionally onstage before entering silent films in the 1910s. He later returned to Broadway and continued working into the television era.

Granby's long career crossed many forms of performance, including radio. Film audiences may also recognize his voice as the Angel Joseph in It's a Wonderful Life, a small role that drew on the same vocal authority heard in his radio work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves three Screen Directors Playhouse performances credited to Granby, two each on Crime Classics, Fibber McGee and Molly and NBC University Theater, plus additional anthology work.

profiles.name: Joyce Gordon
profiles.excerpt: Joyce Gordon was a New York radio repertory actress whose surviving work stretches from Quiet Please and Dimension X to Theater Five.
profiles.bio_html:
Joyce Gordon belonged to the New York radio repertory that supplied actors across mystery, science fiction and adventure programs during the 1940s through the 1960s.

She appeared on Quiet, Please, Dimension X, X Minus One, John Steele, Adventurer and later Theater Five. That span reflects a microphone career able to move with radio drama as its dominant genres changed.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four Theater Five performances credited to Gordon, two each on John Steele, Adventurer, Quiet, Please and X Minus One, plus additional science-fiction and crime work.

profiles.name: Lynn Whitney
profiles.excerpt: Lynn Whitney was a supporting radio actress whose surviving GRH work is concentrated in NBC University Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Lynn Whitney is best documented through the literary and dramatic repertory of NBC University Theater. Personal biography is limited, but the surviving broadcast record shows repeated professional casting.

Her radio work also included appearances on Father Knows Best and Lux Radio Theatre, placing her in family comedy and Hollywood adaptation as well as prestige literary drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten NBC University Theater performances credited to Whitney, plus one appearance each on Father Knows Best and Lux Radio Theatre.

profiles.name: Nelson Olmsted
profiles.excerpt: Nelson Olmsted was a radio actor, storyteller and adapter whose one-man dramatic programs made narration itself a form of repertory performance.
profiles.bio_html:
Nelson Olmsted was born in Minneapolis in 1914 and began broadcasting as a radio announcer in Texas. His ability to create multiple voices quickly led to storytelling programs in which he performed entire casts himself.

Olmsted became NBC's resident storyteller and later created programs including Sleep No More, narrating his own adaptations of horror and science-fiction stories. His work as narrator and adapter was therefore central to his radio identity rather than secondary decoration.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven X Minus One performances credited to Olmsted, two The Chase appearances and additional work on Crime and Peter Chambers, Dimension X and Lights Out.

profiles.name: Patricia Weil
profiles.excerpt: Patricia Weil was a New York radio repertory actress whose surviving work spans wartime drama, science fiction and CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Patricia Weil belongs to the New York radio repertory whose professional record survives most clearly in cast lists and broadcasts. Her credits span several distinct periods of dramatic radio.

Weil appeared on Words at War, X Minus One, Crime and Peter Chambers and Stroke of Fate before later becoming a recurring performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Weil, two each on Crime and Peter Chambers and X Minus One, plus additional anthology work.
